transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-09 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Lisa Monroe (MeridianPay - Head of MLOps), Diego Ramos (MeridianPay - Platform Eng), Rina Patel (MeridianPay - Security), Omar Kwan (MeridianPay - NLP)
Links shared: benchmark-spreadsheet (drive link), security-deck (redwood.com/sec.pdf), kernel-run-logs (s3 link)

Summary: quick sync on latency tuning progress for POC. Reviewed TTFT numbers, streaming changes and sequence-length-driven kernel selection. Agreed on next experiments (kernel compare, raw trace sharing) and security doc follow up.

Topics: TTFT (time to first token), Streaming chunking and backpressure, sequence length distribution and kernel choice (fused-attn, generic kernels), quantization impact (int8), KV cache/prefix caching behavior, dedicated vs hosted routing considerations.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call. we' ll keep to 45 minutes.
[00:12] Lisa Monroe: okay sounds good, Lisa here.
[00:15] Diego Ramos: Diego, hi.
[00:18] Rina Patel: Rina on security.
[00:20] Omar Kwan: Omar here.
[00:22] Priya Rao: Priya from Redwood (SE). alex you want to kick?

[00:30] Alex Chen: yeah thanks. brief agenda: run through last week's benchmark updates, TTFT improvements from streaming + kernel tweaks, plan kernel-sweep for next week, and security follow ups.

[01:05] Priya Rao: quick context - we re focused on reducing time-to-first-token because your user flows are latency sensitive for the auth journey. we ran two changes last week: enabled streaming early flush and switched the kernel scheduler to prefer fused-attn for 256/512 sequences. results are in the sheet.

[01:35] Lisa Monroe: high level we saw p95 drop on the auth flow, but some spikes at start of hour. that's what we want to understand - is it GC, is it cold starts?

[02:00] Priya Rao: right. the headline - TTFT improved from about 320 ms down to ~220 ms on our hosted cluster for typical auth prompts (avg seq ~280). p95 for full response still around 780 ms but p50 is much better. note transcription might show 'K V cash' sometimes in logs, that's just a transcribe artifact - it's KV cache.

[02:30] Diego Ramos: were those numbers from dedicated or hosted? we re trying to map to our expected Dedicated setup.

[02:45] Priya Rao: those were on a Redwood-hosted test pool (same hardware family as your dedicated nodes). we used pinned model variant rwd-7b-q8 with prefix caching enabled. for dedicated we expect similar TTFTs, but things like network MTU and peering can add jitter.

[03:10] Omar Kwan: curious - what changed with streaming early flush? are you chunking tokens differently?

[03:25] Priya Rao: yeah we tune chunk size and early-flush thresholds. basically we send first chunk as soon as generation cross a small token threshold to reduce TTFT. that reduces initial latency at slight cost to throughput efficiency. for your auth flow that's acceptable.

[03:55] Lisa Monroe: the auth flow is very TTFT sensitive - if we can get under 200 ms consistently that'd be ideal.

[04:10] Priya Rao: agreed. two levers: streaming early flush + kernel selection (fused-attn helps SS latency for shorter sequences). second lever is quantization and compilation choices - int8 gives throughput but sometimes increases per-token computation variance.

[04:40] Alex Chen: can we talk kernel choices - Priya you mentioned fused-attn vs generic. what are the tradeoffs?

[04:50] Priya Rao: fused-attn is optimized for short-medium sequence lengths (<=512) and reduces overhead for the attention op. generic kernel is more stable across lengths and works better on longer sequences (>=1024) but has slightly higher per-step overhead. on our test we saw fused-attn cut p50 by ~40 ms for 256 seq. for 1024 seq the fused kernel had marginal benefit, sometimes worse.

[05:30] Diego Ramos: do we have automated selection? we don't want to manually pick kernels per route.

[05:40] Priya Rao: yes runtime has a kernel selector that uses recent sequence-length distribution to pick default kernels; we can pin per-route during rollout. Priya: we can also rig a canary policy to use fused only on auth route.

[06:10] Omar Kwan: said earlier - we have two main workloads: auth (avg seq ~280), statement-summarization (avg seq ~820). looks like fused is good for the auth route, generic for summarization.

[06:35] Lisa Monroe: that's promising. question from security: does streaming early-flush leak partial outputs to logs or change audit trails?

[06:50] Rina Patel: yes we need to ensure every token emission is logged and tied to KMS key usage, since audit requires reconstruction of the full output.

[07:05] Priya Rao: good question. streaming doesn't change what we persist - we still assemble full output server-side and write the canonical response to audit logs. streaming only changes what is pushed to client sooner. KMS/HSM signing and audit entries are the same.

[07:30] Rina Patel: ok please share the security-deck with the exact fields you log.

[07:40] Alex Chen: we'll share redwood.com/sec.pdf and the SOC2 checklist. action item on that.

[07:50] Priya Rao: back to numbers - I ran a quick kernel sweep last night: on auth prompts (n=1k) fused-attn + int8 gave TTFT 210 ms median, p95 ~420ms; fused + q8 (a quant profile) had more stable tail 380ms p95 but slightly worse throughput. generic kernel had median 260ms.

[08:30] Diego Ramos: any memory or OOM risks with fused-attn? our deployment is tight on GPU memory.

[08:40] Priya Rao: fused-attn tends to use a bit more memory due to fusion buffers; however overall quantization reduced memory footprint. we'll run a memory burn test for your exact node type.

[09:05] Lisa Monroe: also noticed cold-start behavior at top of hour - spikes. is that batching/autoscaler related?

[09:20] Priya Rao: likely autoscaler + batch warmup. when request rate spikes from 0 to burst, batching warms up and runtime spins kernels up; that contributes to cold TTFT. two mitigations: keep a hot standby instance (reserved capacity / dedicated) or use predictive warmup (we can keep a tiny pool warm).

[09:55] Alex Chen: that'll be a config in dedicated - reserved min capacity. Diego, are you ok to check reserved window with infra?

[10:10] Diego Ramos: yes I'll confirm.

[10:15] Omar Kwan: on sequence lengths - I've uploaded the sample prompt CSV and distribution to the shared folder this morning. it's biased, but should be good enough for kernel testing.

[10:30] Priya Rao: perfect Omar that helps a lot. we'll run the 256/512/1024 kernel sweep against your prompts so it's realistic.

[10:45] Lisa Monroe: about metrics - can you break TTFT into network + runtime parts? our ops team wants to see where the 60-80ms is going.

[11:00] Priya Rao: yes the benchmark sheet includes a breakdown: client encode + network RTT (measured at our ingress), runtime scheduling + first token generation, and serialization. we'll add a column for peered VPC latencies too.

[11:20] Diego Ramos: one subtle network thing - our peering has MTU 1500 and fragmentation can add ~10-20ms for larger messages; worth accounting.

[11:30] Priya Rao: noted. we'll add a note.

[12:00] Alex Chen: any competitor notes? I know you were evaluating others earlier.

[12:10] Lisa Monroe: we benchmarked OpenAI and Anthropic earlier. OpenAI had lower TTFT for small prompts but less control on VPC/private deployment; Anthropic's p95 was higher. overall Redwood's kernel-level tuning looks promising.

[12:35] Priya Rao: good context. our advantage here is the kernel selector + prefix caching + ability to pin models for dedicated.

[13:00] Rina Patel: security follow ups - we need KMS integration detail (do you support BYOK?), key rotation cadence, and what audit fields you store (full payload, hashes, timestamps).

[13:20] Priya Rao: we support BYOK and HSM-backed KMS. we'll send the detailed KMS integration doc.

[13:40] Alex Chen: ok quick recap and next steps - Alex to share updated benchmark spreadsheet and raw traces, Priya to run kernel sweep for 256/512/1024 with fused vs generic and quant profiles, Diego to confirm VPC peering/MTU and reserved capacity window, Rina to review security docs and post questions, Omar to provide prompt templates and distribution.

[14:10] Lisa Monroe: thanks everyone, sounds good. let's aim to meet same time next week, and if kernel sweep misses targets we'll schedule an SE deep-dive on streaming and compilation.

[14:30] Alex Chen: noted. I'll post the sheet and schedule the next sync for 2027-02-16.

[14:45] Meeting ends.

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., "K V cash" = KV cache). Raw benchmark spreadsheet is authoritative for numbers.
